title: Nonmetal
wiki_lead:
In the context of the periodic table, a nonmetal is a chemical element that mostly lacks distinctive metallic properties. Physically, nonmetals range from colorless gases such as hydrogen to lustrous crystalline solids such as iodine. They are usually less dense than metals and are often poor conductors of heat and electricity. Chemically, they have moderate to very high electronegativity—a tendency to attract electrons in a chemical bond—and their oxides tend to be acidic.
Seventeen elements are widely recognized as nonmetals. Additionally, some or all of six borderline elements (metalloids) are sometimes counted as nonmetals.
The two lightest nonmetals, hydrogen and helium, together make up about 98% of the mass of ordinary matter in the observable universe. Five nonmetallic elements—hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and silicon—make up the bulk of Earth’s atmosphere, oceans, biosphere, and crust. Metals, however, are thought to constitute slightly more than half of Earth’s total mass.
Chemical compounds and alloys involving multiple elements including nonmetals are widespread. Industrial uses of nonmetals as the dominant component include in electronics, combustion, lubrication and machining.
Most nonmetallic elements were identified in the 18th and 19th centuries. While a distinction between metals and other minerals had existed since antiquity, a classification of chemical elements as metallic or nonmetallic emerged only in the late 18th century. Since then about twenty properties have been suggested as criteria for distinguishing nonmetals from metals. In contemporary research usage it is common to use a distinction between metal and not-a-metal based upon the electronic structure of the solids; the elements carbon, arsenic and antimony are then semimetals, a subclass of metals. The rest of the nonmetallic elements are insulators, some of which such as silicon and germanium can readily accommodate dopants that change their electrical conductivity leading to semiconducting behavior.

Definition and applicable elements
Unless otherwise noted, this article describes the stable form of an element at or near standard temperature and pressure (STP).

Nonmetallic chemical elements are often broadly defined as those that largely lack the characteristic properties of metals—namely lustre, malleability, good thermal and electrical conductivity (arising from their electronic band structure), and a general tendency to form basic oxides. There is no widely accepted precise definition based on the extent to which these metallic properties are lacking; any list of nonmetals is therefore open to debate and revision.

grok_lead: Nonmetals are a class of chemical elements located in the upper right portion of the periodic table, characterized by their lack of metallic properties such as luster, malleability, and high electrical and thermal conductivity. There are 17 nonmetal elements, which include hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, selenium, bromine, iodine, and the six noble gases ( helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon). Unlike metals, nonmetals typically exhibit brittleness in solid form, low density, and a tendency to exist as gases, liquids, or dull solids at room temperature, playing essential roles in forming covalent and ionic compounds vital to biological, industrial, and environmental processes. The physical properties of nonmetals vary significantly across the group but generally contrast sharply with those of metals: they are poor conductors of heat and electricity, often brittle and non-ductile when solid, and have lower melting and boiling points. For example, common nonmetals like oxygen and nitrogen are colorless gases, bromine is a reddish-brown liquid, and elements such as carbon (in diamond or graphite form) and sulfur are solids that lack metallic sheen. These properties arise from their electronic structures, where valence electrons are tightly held, leading to localized bonding rather than delocalized metallic bonds. Chemically, nonmetals are highly electronegative and reactive, particularly the halogens in group 17 ( fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine), which readily gain one electron to form anions and produce acidic oxides or compounds like hydrochloric acid. Other nonmetals, such as carbon and phosphorus, form extensive covalent networks or molecules, enabling the creation of organic compounds and biomolecules. In contrast, the noble gases are chemically inert due to their stable, filled electron shells, though some like xenon can form compounds under extreme conditions. This diversity in reactivity underscores nonmetals' importance in oxidation-reduction reactions, acid-base chemistry, and the formation of nearly all known compounds. The classification of elements into metals and nonmetals originated with early periodic table developments and remains fundamental to understanding periodic trends, such as increasing electronegativity from left to right across periods. Nonmetals' distinct behaviors also influence their applications, from oxygen in respiration to silicon (bordering nonmetals but often classified separately) in semiconductors, though the core group excludes metalloids like boron and silicon.
